title: Binary Search: Search a Rotated Sorted Array
oneLiner: A sorted array that was rotated is no longer sorted, but whichever way you cut it at the midpoint, at least one half still is.
keyTakeaway: Cut a rotated sorted array at any midpoint and at least one of the two halves is fully sorted. Compare nums[lo] with nums[mid] to find out which one, then check whether the target falls inside that sorted half's range. If it does, search there; if not, it can only be in the other half. Either way half the range is gone after one comparison, so it stays O(log n).
explanation:
Take a sorted array of distinct integers and rotate it: [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7] rotated by 4 becomes [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. Given the rotated array and a target, return the target's index, or -1 if it isn't there, in O(log n). A linear scan is O(n), and plain binary search breaks: at the midpoint 7 with target 0, "0 is smaller than 7, go left" sends you the wrong way.

The array is two sorted runs glued together, with one drop between them (7 to 0 above). Any midpoint falls in one of the runs, so the drop is on at most one side of mid. That means at least one of [lo, mid] and [mid, hi] contains no drop and is sorted. You can tell which with one comparison: if nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted; otherwise the drop is on the left, so the right half is sorted.

A sorted half is useful because you can test membership by its endpoints. If the left half is sorted and nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid], the target can only be on the left, so set hi = mid - 1. Otherwise it can only be on the right, so set lo = mid + 1. The mirror rule applies when the right half is sorted: if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi], go right, else go left. You never need to know where the rotation point is; each step just asks which half is the clean one.

Use the inclusive loop (while lo <= hi) and check nums[mid] == target first, exactly as in Binary Search: Find a Target. The <= in nums[lo] <= nums[mid] matters when lo == mid (a range of one or two elements): then the "left half" is just nums[lo], which is trivially sorted. Common follow-ups: find the minimum of a rotated array (the same half test, but you move toward the unsorted side, where the drop is), find the rotation count (the index of that minimum), and the version with duplicates, where nums[lo] == nums[mid] no longer tells you which half is sorted and the worst case degrades to O(n) because you can only shrink lo by one.

The visualization searches [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] for 0. Each step highlights the sorted half that the decision is based on.

def search_rotated(nums, target):

    # If nums[mid] == target, return mid. If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half
    # is sorted: go left if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid], else go right.
    # Otherwise the right half is sorted: go right if
    # nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi], else go left. Return -1 if not found.
    return 0

visualizationSteps.message: Search for 0. The array is sorted but rotated: 7 then 0 is the one drop. lo = 0, hi = 6.
mid = 3. nums[lo] = 4 <= nums[mid] = 7, so the left half [0..3] is sorted. Is 0 in its range [4, 7)? No.
So the target can only be in the other half. Keep [4..6].
mid = 5. nums[lo] = 0 <= nums[mid] = 1, so the left half [4..5] is sorted. Is 0 in its range [0, 1)? Yes.
So the target can only be in the sorted half. Keep [4..4].

recognitionSignals: "Sorted, then rotated" (or shifted, or wrapped around) at an unknown pivot, plus a requirement of O(log n).
The array is almost sorted except for one drop, and you need to find a value or the drop itself.
gotchas: Using < instead of <= in nums[lo] <= nums[mid]: when lo == mid the left half is one element and is sorted, and getting this wrong sends two-element searches like [3, 1] for 1 the wrong way.

The range checks must include the known end and exclude mid: nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid] for the left half, nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi] for the right. mid was already checked, so its side of the comparison doesn't matter, but dropping the = at lo or hi misses targets sitting at the ends.
This trick needs DISTINCT values. With duplicates, nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] can't tell you which half is sorted, and you have to fall back to lo++.
confusableWith: Binary Search: Find a Target (this track) works on a fully sorted array, where comparing target with nums[mid] alone picks the side. Here that comparison is not enough; you first have to find the sorted half.

Binary Search on Answer: Minimum Eating Speed (this track) also bends binary search to a problem that doesn't look sorted, but it searches a range of candidate answers with a feasibility check. This one still searches array indices.

complexity.note: Every step discards half the range after checking which half is sorted, so about log₂ n steps; only lo, hi and mid are stored.
